Jensen may need to update the bottle.

Last year, Jensen Huang famously gave Nscale CEO Josh Payne a bottle of Johnnie Walker inscribed “$0 to $50 billion in 18 months.” With Nscale now reportedly targeting a ~$30-35B IPO valuation, we went through the new $NSCL S-1 to update our $IREN comp.

At that valuation, IREN doesn't look as obviously cheap. On headline backlog multiples, Nscale is actually cheaper.

>Nscale: $30-35B / $103.4B TCV (Total Contract Value) = 0.29-0.34x
>IREN today: ~$20B EV / ~$16B TCV = ~1.25x
>IREN at its YE27 target of 800MW leased / ~$48B TCV = ~0.42x
>At Jensen's $50B marker, IREN looked a bit cheaper on forward TCV: ~0.42x vs ~0.48x. At $30-35B for Nscale, it's the other way around: ~0.29-0.34x vs ~0.42x for IREN.

But there are some pretty big differences in what sits behind those numbers:

Nscale's contracts average 5.7 years vs ~3 years for IREN, so every leased MW naturally produces a lot more TCV. And >80% of Nscale TCV comes from Microsoft + Anthropic, with Anthropic alone accounting for up to $44.6B, or ~43%. IREN is concentrated too: Microsoft is roughly half of its current contracted backlog, but that concentration should fall materially as IREN approaches its 800MW leased target.

The major question is how much infrastructure still needs to materialize to monetize the backlog: Nscale has ~1.37GW of active/contracted capacity today, but fulfilling its $103B TCV requires substantially more power to come online. Its plan to reach 8-10GW also relies heavily on BTM generation, adding cost and execution risk.

The Anthropic contracts are a good example: Nscale says it has no binding commitments for the financing required, Anthropic can terminate a late tranche without liability, and Nscale generally doesn't lock up equipment through long-term supply agreements, instead ordering largely just-in-time.

IREN has the opposite problem. It still needs to lease the capacity, but has >2GW of energized/approved power behind the story already. Its 2026-27 contracted builds are also ~90-95% covered by GPU financing and customer prepayments, although the broader buildout obviously still requires a huge amount of capital.

So Nscale at $30-35B is cheaper on headline forward TCV. The question is how much of a discount that $103B deserves for duration, concentration and the power/financing still required to deliver it.

IREN has the opposite problem. It still needs to lease the capacity, but has >2GW of energized/approved power behind the story already. Its 2026-27 contracted builds are also ~90-95% covered by GPU financing and customer prepayments, although the broader buildout obviously still requires a huge amount of capital.
